query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning model that leverages multiscale descriptors derived from the hierarchical heterostructure (capturing features such as phase distribution, interface characteristics, and local stiffness variations inferred from DFT-calculated atomic interactions) will enable rapid and more accurate prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing compared to conventional simulation approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure with multiple length-scale features (e.g., nano- to micro-scale interfaces and phase domains).
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a machine-learning framework that integrates microstructural descriptors (from microscopy and EBSD) with atomic-level interaction data (e.g., from DFT) to predict mechanical properties.
generation.conditions: Standard tensile and fracture testing conditions (room temperature, controlled strain rates) on well-characterized HfNbTiVAl10 samples; the microstructural characterization must adequately capture the hierarchical features.
generation.structural_mediator: The hierarchical heterostructure mediates the mechanical response by influencing local stiffness, stress distribution, and initiation of plastic deformation or fracture at interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Microstructure-derived descriptors capture variations in local elastic properties, yield initiation thresholds, and potential fracture initiation sites. By combining these descriptors with DFT-calculated atomic interactions in a machine-learning model, the model can predict macroscopic mechanical behavior more efficiently than full-scale simulation methods that explicitly resolve every microstructural detail.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated model is expected to yield predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness with an accuracy improvement (potentially 10–20% more accurate) and reduced computation time (by roughly an order of magnitude) compared to traditional simulation approaches.
generation.baseline: Existing simulation methods, such as full-scale DFT/molecular dynamics or continuum models that require extensive computational resources and time for multiscale resolution.
generation.boundary: The predictive improvements may not hold if (1) the hierarchical descriptors do not fully capture all relevant microstructural features, (2) the alloy exhibits unanticipated deformation mechanisms (e.g., at extreme strain rates or temperatures), or (3) there is significant variation in the material’s heterostructure that falls outside the training data of the model.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of predictive accuracy gains and computational speedup is uncertain until the machine-learning model is calibrated against a comprehensive dataset. Moreover, variations in processing or testing conditions may lead to deviations from the predicted performance improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple HfNbTiVAl10 specimens and perform detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, EBSD) to extract relevant hierarchical descriptors. Independently, perform standard tensile and fracture tests to obtain experimental values for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness. Develop a machine-learning model using the microstructural descriptors combined with selected DFT-calculated atomic interaction parameters, then compare the model predictions against the experimental measurements and against predictions from established simulation approaches.
measurements: Fracture toughness values from standardized fracture tests
Microstructural descriptor parameters (grain size, phase/interface distributions, etc.)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine-learning model does not achieve at least a 10–20% improvement in accuracy or reduce computational time by roughly one order of magnitude compared to established simulation methods under defined testing conditions, or if its predictions fail to reliably match experimental measurements, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Atomic Interaction-Based Prediction of Phase Formations in High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are of particular interest due to their unique combination of high strength, ductility, and fracture resistance. These properties are largely impacted by the phases and number of phases present in the alloy. Due to the enormous chemical design space, with typically five or six elements present in the alloys in addition to the various processing parameters, the prediction of the number of phases is challenging. While there have been multiple recent reports of phase predictions through data-driven models, an alternate approach is proposed and demonstrated here. In this work, phase prediction is performed using features derived from DFT-calculated pairwise interactions among constituent elements (incorporating bonding and structure) rather than relying solely on traditional elemental descriptors such as electronegativity. By focusing on atomic interaction features, our model provides a novel perspective on the phase stability in HEAs. Predicting Elastic Constants of Refractory Complex Concentrated Alloys Using Machine Learning Approach

Abstract: AbstractRefractory complex concentrated alloys (RCCAs) have drawn increasing attention recently owing to their balanced mechanical properties, including excellent creep resistance, ductility, and oxidation resistance. The mechanical and thermal properties of RCCAs are directly linked with the elastic constants. However, it is time consuming and expensive to obtain the elastic constants of RCCAs with conventional trial-and-error experiments. The elastic constants of RCCAs are predicted using a combination of density functional theory simulation data and machine learning (ML) algorithms in this study. The elastic constants of several RCCAs are predicted using the random forest regressor, gradient boosting regressor (GBR), and XGBoost regression models. Based on performance metrics R-squared, mean average error and root mean square error, the GBR model was found to be most promising in predicting the elastic constant of RCCAs among the three ML models.
